analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 12% for two years.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap credit card rates at 12% was introduced in October 2001 with no cosponsors, sent to a House committee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Max Sandlin's bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act to bar credit card companies from charging more than 12% annual interest on card balances for two years, starting 60 days after the law's passage [S3]. The cap was temporary — it would have expired after two years [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its subcommittee on financial institutions, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households carrying credit card debt. Any cardholder who revolved a balance would have paid sharply less interest while the cap was in effect; with typical card rates in the late teens or higher at the time, a 12% cap would have cut finance charges on existing balances substantially.

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred the annual percentage rate on any outstanding credit card balance under an open-end credit plan from exceeding 12 percent, effective 60 days after enactment and lasting two years [S2][S3].
Because the cap applied to credit outstanding on card accounts, it would have lowered the cost of carrying balances people already owe, not just new purchases [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and finance companies that earn interest on revolving balances — would have lost revenue on every card balance above 12% interest. Card issuers might also have tightened credit terms, cut rewards, or added fees to make up part of the lost interest income.

drawbacks.text: A binding rate cap can reduce access to credit: issuers who cannot price for risk may raise fees, tighten approval standards, or stop lending to weaker-credit borrowers, who could lose access to cards entirely (general policy mechanism; not stated in the bill text [S3]).
The cap was temporary — two years from enactment — so it offered borrowers short-term relief without a permanent rate limit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households with revolving credit card debt, the upside was direct and large: interest charges on existing balances would fall while the cap lasted. The main cost falls on card issuers, and the standard trade-off — some borrowers facing tighter credit access or higher fees — is real but speculative in degree. On balance the bill was a straightforward consumer-protection measure aimed at an industry charging rates well above 12% at the time.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing and no vote until that Congress ended in January 2003 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Max Sandlin introduced the Credit Card Fairness Act on October 12, 2001 [S1][S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S5].
On November 2, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with no cosponsors, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept charging market interest rates on card balances, unburdened by a 12% cap; cardholders with revolving debt got no relief.

for.name: Rep. Max Sandlin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill capping credit card rates at 12% and referred it to committee; no other member signed on.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican; the bill's only committee stop
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 12, 2001, sent it to the Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee, and took no further action — no hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill's only support was its single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split shows up in the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and consumer finance companies)
industries.note: The bill would have capped the interest they can charge on outstanding card balances at 12% for two years, cutting revenue on every balance above that rate. Their interest ran against cardholders' interest in cheaper debt [S2][S3].
